_note: v1 prompts (2026-09-06), gemini-2.5-flash-image. This subject is a ROCK, so none of the four styles is a micrograph of an organism. The set walks one scale ladder: 3d = the hand specimen (what it actually is), textbook = a cutaway through the rock down to one carbonate globule plus the fracture-surface texture (where the claim came from), watercolor = the carbonate globule in cross-section as a mineralogical plate, sem = the nanometre-scale segmented ridge, which is the modality the 1996 image actually is. Every prompt describes the segmented shape POSITIVELY as welded mineral relief — 'a row of tiny nodules fused end to end, flush in the surface, no gap and no shadow underneath' — because naming what it must not look like would reinforce it. The words tube, rod, worm, body, capsule and organism are deliberately absent from all four prompts. The magnesite rim's outward-projecting crystal facets are in the textbook and watercolor prompts specifically because a crystalline sawtooth edge cannot be misread as a membrane.
_do_not_draw_summary: no cell body, membrane, organelles or appendages; no glow; no planets, starfields, rovers or aliens; no lettering; no border or frame.
textbook: Clean cutaway textbook illustration of a broken block of METEORITE ROCK — a mineral specimen. Square 1:1, 1080x1080, a plain neutral dark charcoal background reaching all four edges of the square. Refined educational-plate look: muted, slightly desaturated dusty tints, THIN clean dark-brown pen-weight contours (never heavy black cartoon strokes), and soft painterly shading WITHIN each individual crystal grain so every grain has its own gentle light and shade and the whole face has subtle dimensionality rather than flat fills, each mineral its own distinct soft fill. Composition: one chunky rectangular slab of stone, about half again as wide as it is tall, tilted a little to the left, filling roughly three quarters of the frame, its broad top face turned toward us. The stone is one single uniform material all the way through, formed by crystals growing together in a melt, so the SAME coarse mosaic of angular interlocking greenish-grey crystal grains covers the top face AND continues unchanged down every cut side of the block, in the same colours and the same random jumble of orientations, with no horizontal layers, no bedding, no stripes and no change of colour from top to side. The grains are of clearly different sizes from small chips to broad plates, meeting along straight edges at sharp corners, with scattered small solid black specks and fine hairline cracks. One narrow crack runs across the top face on a shallow diagonal all the way from the slab's left edge to its right edge, entering the carbonate concretion on one side and leaving it on the other and carrying on to the rim of the slab. Sitting on that crack, low and to the LEFT of centre, is one small squat carbonate concretion seen in cross-section — a rounded oval only a little wider than it is tall, about one SIXTH as wide as the slab, its long axis lying along the crack. The concretion is CUT FLUSH with the rock face: its bands lie in exactly the same flat plane as the grains around it, the stone comes right up against its outer ring, and it casts no shadow and stands no higher than the surrounding surface — it is a slice through something inside the stone, not a disc placed on top of it. Its concentric bands, counted from the very middle outwards, are exactly these five, in this order: first the middle itself, a dark burnt-orange; second, a paler apricot band around it; third, a narrow near-black band flecked with tiny charcoal grains; fourth, a cream-white band; and fifth and outermost, one more narrow near-black band. The warmest colour is in the middle and the darkest ring is on the outside, the way the rings run in a cut agate. Along only about a third of its circumference, in two or three short irregular stretches, a few small blunt crystal facets poke out sideways from the outermost ring into the surrounding stone; the rest of its edge is a plain smooth curve. In the UPPER RIGHT quarter of the same face, well away from the concretion, a patch of the stone is finely knobbly like coarse sand set in concrete. Within that patch, one low welt is HALF SUNK into the grit: a short row of tiny mineral knobs fused end to end, with the grit banked up against both of its flanks so its outline disappears into the surrounding grains, no shadow anywhere beneath it, painted in exactly the same sandy greys and the same thin contour as the grit around it. It is a swelling of the surface, not a thing resting on it. Leave generous plain charcoal outside the slab and plain rock face between the structures so labels can attach. Everything is dry, matte, mineral and solid. Keep the picture free of any lettering, digits, scale bars, arrows or watermarks.
sem: Photorealistic false-colour scanning electron micrograph of a freshly broken MINERAL SURFACE inside a stony meteorite, filling the whole square 1:1 1080x1080 frame edge to edge with no border, frame or letterbox. The entire frame, corner to corner, is one continuous rough crust of stone, with no smooth ground and no flat plate anywhere in it: a dense cauliflower-like botryoidal encrustation of blunt broken knobs and angular crystal facets of many sizes, jammed against each other and fused together, piled into mounds and terraces, split by deep shadowed clefts, with splintered plates and blocky shards jutting out of the pile at all angles. Think of a close-up of popcorn-textured concrete rubble, or of coral rock, filling every square millimetre of the picture. Strong raking light from the upper left so the mounds cast long shadows and the relief reads as a rugged three-dimensional landscape. Running diagonally across the middle of the frame, from lower left toward upper right, is one long low RIDGE made of the very same crust: a single row of knobs fused end to end into a gently curved raised welt, thicker near the middle and tapering away at both ends, its lower half buried in the crust so the surrounding knobs bank up against its flanks and it merges into them along its whole length, with no gap and no shadow beneath it. It is a swelling of the crust, not an object lying on the crust. The false colour follows the HEIGHT of the surface and nothing else: everything low in the clefts is deep slate blue-grey, everything mid-height is steel grey, and every high point is warm ochre to pale sand, with a smooth continuous gradient between them, so the colour changes only as the surface rises and never marks out a separate object. The ridge takes its colour from the same gradient and so is the same ochre as every other high point. Shallow depth of field: the ridge is crisp, the far upper corner falls softly out of focus. Cool studio microscopy lighting, matte dry dusty crystalline texture throughout. Everything in the frame is stone. Keep the picture free of any lettering, digits, scale bars, arrows or watermarks.

A soft sepia wash enters at the LOWER LEFT corner and drifts on a diagonal toward the upper right, fading as it goes, like an old tea stain that ran across the sheet; it is an uneven blotch that never closes into a ring. The slab is painted very large and CROPPED by the picture: its stone continues straight off the left edge and straight off the bottom edge of the square, so there is no paper at all showing in the lower left corner, and the slab covers well over half the sheet. Only its upper and right margins end on the paper, as ragged straight broken edges meeting at sharp corners, with bare paper beyond them. Its face is a mosaic of interlocking grains in soft greenish-grey and olive washes, of clearly different sizes from small chips to broad plates, each bounded by straight fine brown ink edges meeting at sharp corners, with a scatter of small solid black flecks. One thin dark crack runs right across the slab on a shallow diagonal and continues off the picture at both ends. Sitting inside that crack, above and right of the middle of the slab, is one small squat carbonate concretion in cross-section — a rounded oval only a little wider than it is tall, about one sixth as wide as the visible slab, its long axis lying along the crack. Its concentric bands, counted from the very middle outwards, are exactly these five, in this order: first the middle itself, a dark burnt-orange; second, a paler apricot band around it; third, a narrow near-black band flecked with tiny charcoal grains; fourth, a cream-white band; and fifth and outermost of all, one more narrow near-black band. The warmest colour is therefore in the middle and the darkest ring is on the outside, the way the rings run in a cut agate. Where that outermost ring meets the surrounding stone it breaks into a fine sawtooth of small crystal facets pointing outwards. Soft translucent washes, visible brush texture, fine confident linework, dry matte mineral surfaces throughout, the paint running right off the edges of the square. The entire frame, corner to corner, is one continuous rough crust of stone, with no smooth ground and no flat plate anywhere in it: a dense cauliflower-like botryoidal encrustation of blunt broken knobs and angular crystal facets of many sizes, jammed against each other and fused together, piled into mounds and terraces, split by deep shadowed clefts, with splintered plates and blocky shards jutting out of the pile at all angles. Think of a close-up of popcorn-textured concrete rubble, or of coral rock, filling every square millimetre of the picture. Strong raking light from the upper left so the mounds cast long shadows and the relief reads as a rugged three-dimensional landscape. Running diagonally across the middle of the frame, from lower left toward upper right, is one long low RIDGE made of the very same crust: a single row of knobs fused end to end into a gently curved raised welt, thicker near the middle and tapering away at both ends, its lower half buried in the crust so the surrounding knobs bank up against its flanks and it merges into them along its whole length, with no gap and no shadow beneath it. It is a swelling of the crust, not an object lying on the crust. The false colour follows the HEIGHT of the surface and nothing else: everything low in the clefts is deep slate blue-grey, everything mid-height is steel grey, and every high point is warm ochre to pale sand, with a smooth continuous gradient between them, so the colour changes only as the surface rises and never marks out a separate object. The ridge takes its colour from the same gradient and so is the same ochre as every other high point. Shallow depth of field: the ridge is crisp, the far upper corner falls softly out of focus. Cool studio microscopy lighting, matte dry dusty crystalline texture throughout. Everything in the frame is stone. Keep the picture free of any lettering, digits, scale bars, arrows or watermarks.
_v4.3d: Semi-realistic museum-specimen still of a single ROCK — a stony meteorite — photographed as a study object. Square 1:1, 1080x1080. A clean seamless pale warm-grey studio background reaches all four edges of the square, with a soft contact shadow directly under the stone. Soft global illumination from the upper left, gentle rim light, matte materials, no gloss and no reflections. The stone is a big angular loaf-shaped lump, clearly WIDER than it is tall — about half again as wide — resting on its flattest side and spanning roughly four fifths of the width of the square. Its outside is a matte dark grey-brown skin that is distinctly HACKLY and torn: shallow scooped hollows, blunt raised ridges, small stepped flakes lifting at their edges and a coarse sandpaper grain over all of it, dulled by pale beige dust the way a stone looks after long burial in ice. It is a rough, chipped, weathered crust, not a smooth rounded river pebble. Over the right-hand third that crust has flaked away in a ragged step, and the fresh break exposes the inside as a TIGHTLY INTERLOCKING crystalline mass: greenish-grey blocky crystals a few millimetres across, wedged hard against one another with no cavity and no gap between them, every grain sharing its whole edge with its neighbours like broken paving stones pressed together, tilted at many different angles so some flash a small hard glint on a flat cleavage face while their neighbours lie in shadow. Sizes range from little chips to broad slabs; scattered tiny solid black specks and a few small dull orange-brown flecks sit along the grain boundaries; fine hairline cracks run across the break. Natural, believable stone colours — grey-brown outside, green-grey inside — neither neon nor near-monochrome. One stone only, nothing else on the surface beside it.
